prerequisite_rule: Needs the Heat: Pedal to the Metal base game.
what_it_adds: Two new tracks (Japan with rain puddles that limit downshifting, Mexico with chicanes), the 1964 Championship season, Air Intake upgrade cards for extra cooling, and a 7th car (orange) with its own deck and mat.
what_it_fixes: Base tracks start to feel familiar; adds two very different circuits, a strong all-round upgrade, and room for a seventh player.
verdict_reason: Most replies in BGG's "which expansion?" thread picked Heavy Rain over Tunnel Vision: rain puddles are easy to grasp and Air Intake cooling is useful on every track.
notes: Not standalone. Everything except the new track board fits in the base game box, even sleeved (BGG review).

prerequisite_rule: Needs the Heat: Pedal to the Metal base game.
what_it_adds: Two new tracks (Spain with tunnels where you can't discard, the Netherlands with chicanes), the 1965 Championship season, Front Wing upgrades with the new Draft move, and an extra car (purple) for one more player.
what_it_fixes: Adds a reliable slipstream strategy for groups that always pick the same upgrades, plus more tracks for building custom championships.
verdict_reason: BGG reviewers call it a close twin of Heavy Rain: just as good if you want more tracks, but slightly less fresh, so most suggest it second.
notes: Not standalone. With Heavy Rain it allows 8 racers on track; reviewers note 8 cars can feel crowded in tight corners.

prerequisite_rule: Needs the Heat: Pedal to the Metal base game.
what_it_adds: Two new tracks (South Africa with loose gravel, Germany with chicanes on a long straight), the 1966 Championship season, Sliding Skirts upgrades, and an extra car with its own deck and mat.
what_it_fixes: Gives groups who have played every track another two circuits and a new upgrade type, plus more cars to pick from.
verdict_reason: Same formula as the first two boxes; BGG first impressions frame it as more of what fans already like, best once your group is hooked on Heat.
notes: Not standalone. Early printings had a sponsor card misprint; Days of Wonder posted an erratum on BGG.

prerequisite_rule: Needs the Heat: Pedal to the Metal base game.
what_it_adds: Card pack only: new Legend cards at three difficulty levels covering every car color, Power Up cards that give Legends abilities like slipstream and draft, Rival cards, and new Sponsorship cards.
what_it_fixes: Base-game Legends (bots) get too easy for experienced players and only cover base-game colors; this makes bots tougher, adjustable, and usable with the expansion cars.
verdict_reason: BGG's top review calls it essential if you race against bots, but several fans in the announcement thread said they'd pass because they rarely use Legends.
notes: No new cars or tracks: to field the orange, purple and Rocky Roads cars as Legends you need those expansions. Days of Wonder says it works with Heavy Rain, Tunnel Vision and Rocky Roads.

what_it_adds: Two modules: The Cities (3 of 7 double-sided city tiles replace the race to 15 points; first to meet a city's points-and-cards goal wins) and The Trading Posts (20 tiles that grant permanent bonuses, like an extra gem or extra noble points, once you own the right cards).
what_it_fixes: Every game of base Splendor ends the same way, racing to 15 points; city goals give each game a different target while turns stay just as quick.
verdict_reason: BGG reviewers call it variety without added complexity: easy to teach to new players and it doesn't make games longer. The Cities module is the favourite.
notes: Updated re-release of the Cities and Trading Posts modules from the 2017 Cities of Splendor box, with small rule changes. If you already own Cities of Splendor you already have these modules. The two modules can be played on their own or together, and combined with The Sun Never Sets. Amazon's listing title swaps the module names; the box contains Cities and Trading Posts.

what_it_adds: Two modules: The Orient (30 extra development cards, 10 per level, with special powers like double bonuses, wild-colour bonuses and chaining into a free card) and Strongholds (3 towers per player that lock face-up cards; put all 3 on one card and you can buy it as an extra action).
what_it_fixes: Base Splendor has almost no direct interaction; Strongholds let you block and claim cards, and Orient cards let you chain big turns, so it plays more like a real engine-builder.
verdict_reason: A BGG reviewer who disliked these modules in Cities of Splendor found that Orient plus Strongholds together add real timing tricks and blocking, but more to think about than The Silk Road.
notes: Updated re-release of the Orient and Strongholds modules from the 2017 Cities of Splendor box. Owners of Cities of Splendor already have these modules. Can be combined with The Silk Road. Amazon's listing title swaps the module names; the box contains Orient and Strongholds.

prerequisite_rule: Requires the Sagrada base game (Remastered or original).
what_it_adds: Three modules: 5-6 player support (extra dice, two player boards, dice tray); Lightboards giving each player a personal 10-die reserve plus 6 new tool cards; Focal Point private objectives and Panorama objectives shared with your neighbours.
what_it_fixes: Lets 5-6 people play and adds more control over the luck of the dice draft.
verdict_reason: If your group ever has more than four players, this is the one to get. The Lightboards also give you more choice each turn, so it's a good pick even at smaller counts.
notes: Replaces the out-of-print Sagrada 5-6 Player Expansion. Panorama objectives need 3+ players. Lightboards don't fit the Remastered insert.

what_it_adds: Apprentice cards, Masterwork dice that score prestige for meeting tricky restrictions, and Toil public objectives.
what_it_fixes: Adds new goals and a way to reward risky placements when the base game starts to feel samey.
verdict_reason: Players often name Life's Toil objectives among their favourite modules. It adds variety without slowing the game much, so it's the safest Great Facades box to start with.
notes: Great Facades 2 of 3. Works with Sagrada Remastered, but its cards use the older smaller card size.

what_it_adds: Inspiration cards that give players special powers, Rare Glass dice with new private objectives, and symmetry/balance public objectives.
what_it_fixes: Gives players unique powers and more ways to score, which adds variety to repeat plays.
verdict_reason: Inspiration cards and the Symmetry objectives are fan favourites. It's a good second box, but it's harder to find now than Life or Glory.
notes: Great Facades 1 of 3. Out of stock at the publisher store as of checked_on; look for it at other retailers. Works with Remastered, but uses the older card size.

what_it_adds: Strife dice, Pioneer cards that reward being first to meet objectives, Flourish private objectives, and Rivalry public objectives.
what_it_fixes: Adds more direct competition to a game that otherwise feels like everyone is solving their own puzzle.
verdict_reason: Get this if your group wants to race and compete with each other. If you like Sagrada as a calm puzzle, Life or Passion is the better buy.
notes: Great Facades 3 of 3 (final). Rivalry objectives work better at higher player counts. Works with Remastered, but uses the older card size.

what_it_adds: Every promo window pattern card released from 2017 to 2025, plus a new foil exclusive.
what_it_fixes: Adds more window patterns for variety.
verdict_reason: These are just extra window patterns. Only worth it if you've played the base patterns to death or you collect Sagrada promos.
notes: The publisher URL handle says 2026, but the product is named the 2025 Promo Pack.

what_it_adds: Six new foil promo window pattern cards.
what_it_fixes: Adds a few new window patterns.
verdict_reason: It's a cheap add-on, but it's only six cards. Grab it if you're already ordering from Floodgate.
